title: Homily II — Adam, Eve and the saints call to her

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily II on the Dormition, cols. 733-736 (PDF leaves 408-409)

source_text: Τότε δὴ, τότε Ἀδὰμ καὶ Εὔα, οἱ τοῦ γένους προπάτορες, ἀγαλλομένοις τοῖς χείλεσι διαπρυσίως ἀνακεκράγασι· Σὺ μακαρία, θύγατερ, τῆς παραβάσεως ἡμῖν τὰ ἐπιτίμια λέλυκας. Σὺ φθαρτὸν ἐξ ἡμῶν σῶμα κληρονομήσασα, ἀφθαρσίας ἡμῖν ἐκυοφόρησας ἔνδυμα. Σὺ τὸ εἶναι ἐξ ἡμετέρας ὀσφύος ἁρπάσασα, τὸ εὖ εἶναι ἡμῖν ἀνταπέδωκας· τὰς ὠδῖνας ἔλυσας· τὰ τοῦ θανάτου διέῤῥηξας σπάργανα· τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἡμῖν ἀποκατέστησας ἐνδιαίτημα. Ἡμεῖς ἐκλείσαμεν τὸν παράδεισον, σὺ τοῦ τῆς ζωῆς ξύλου τὴν εἴσοδον ἀνεπέτασας. Ἐκ τῶν χρηστῶν δι' ἡμῶν ἦλθε τὰ λυπηρά· διὰ σοῦ ἐκ τῶν λυπηρῶν ἐπανῆλθεν ἡμῖν τὰ χρηστότερα. Καὶ πῶς θανάτου γεύσῃ, ἡ ἄχραντος; Σοὶ πρὸς ζωὴν γέφυρα, καὶ κλίμαξ πρὸς οὐρανόν· καὶ πρὸς ἀθανασίαν ὁ θάνατος πορθμεῖον γενήσεται. Ὄντως μακαρία σὺ, παμμακάριστε. Τίς γὰρ, εἰ μήτιγε ὁ Λόγος ᾖ, προσενήνεκται τοῦτο πάσχων, ὃ πράττειν ὑπείληπται; Ἐπεκρότει δὲ καὶ πᾶς ὁ τῶν ἁγίων χορός· Σὺ ἡμῶν τὰς προῤῥήσεις πεπλήρωκας. Σὺ ἡμῖν τὴν καραδοκουμένην εὐφροσύνην προσήνεγκας. Διὰ σοῦ γὰρ δεσμῶν θανάτου λελύμεθα. Δεῦρο πρὸς ἡμᾶς, ὦ θεῖον καὶ ζωηφόρον κειμήλιον. Ἐλθὲ ποθοῦσιν ἡμῖν, ἡ τὸν πόθον ἡμῶν ἐκπεράνασα. Ἀλλ' ἀνθεῖλκε λόγοις οὐχ ἧττοσιν τῶν ἐν σώματι περιεστώτων ἁγίων πληθύς· Μεῖνον μεθ' ἡμῶν, ἡ ἡμετέρα παράκλησις, λέγουσα· τὸ μόνον ἐπὶ γῆς ἡμῶν παραμύθιον. Μὴ ἐάσῃς ἡμᾶς ὀρφανοὺς, ἡ Μήτηρ, τοῦ συμπαθοῦς τοῦ Υἱοῦ σου προκινδυνεύοντας. Ἔχοιμέν σε τῶν πόνων ἀνάπαυλαν, καὶ τῶν ἱδρώτων ἀνάπτυξιν. Σοὶ καὶ μένειν θελούσῃ τὸ δύνασθαι πάρεστι, καὶ ἀπαίρειν προθυμουμένῃ οὐδὲν ἐμπόδιον. Εἰ ἀπαίρεις, ἡ τοῦ Θεοῦ σκηνὴ, καὶ ἡμεῖς συναπαίροιμεν, ὁ σὸς λαὸς διὰ τὸν σὸν Υἱὸν χρηματίσαντες. Σὲ μόνην ἐπὶ γῆς καταλελειμμένην ἡμῖν παρηγορίαν κεκτήμεθα. Σοὶ καὶ ζώσῃ συζῆν, καὶ θνησκούσῃ συνθνήσκειν μακάριον. Τί δὲ θνησκούσῃ φαμέν; Σοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ὁ θάνατος, καὶ ζωὴ κρείττων, καὶ ταύτην τὴν ζωὴν ἀπαραβλήτοις συγκρίσεσιν ὑπεραίρουσα· ἡμῖν δὲ πῶς ὁ βίος ἀβίωτος, σὲ μὴ κεκτημένοις συνόμιλον;
pass_a_gloss: Then indeed, then Adam and Eve, the forefathers of the race, with exulting lips cried out (ἀνακράζω) piercingly: You, blessed (μακαρία) daughter, have loosed (λύω) for us the penalties (ἐπιτίμια) of the transgression. You, having inherited from us a corruptible (φθαρτός) body, carried in womb (κυοφορέω) for us a garment (ἔνδυμα) of incorruption (ἀφθαρσία). You, having seized (ἁρπάζω) being (τὸ εἶναι) from our loin (ὀσφύς), gave back in return to us well-being; you loosed the pangs (ὠδῖνες); you tore apart the swaddling bands (σπάργανα) of death; you restored to us the ancient dwelling. We shut (κλείω) paradise; you opened the entrance (εἴσοδος) of the tree of life. Out of good things through us came the grievous things (τὰ λυπηρά); through you out of the grievous things the better things returned to us. And how will you taste (γεύομαι) death, the spotless one (ἄχραντος)? To you a bridge (γέφυρα) to life, and a ladder (κλίμαξ) to heaven, and toward immortality (ἀθανασία) death will become a ferry (πορθμεῖον). Truly blessed you, all-blessed. For who, unless (εἰ μήτιγε) it be the Word, has been brought forward/has borne himself suffering (πάσχω) this which he is supposed/undertaken to do (πράττω)? And the whole choir (χορός) of the saints applauded (ἐπικροτέω): You have fulfilled (πληρόω) our predictions. You have brought (προσφέρω) us the awaited (καραδοκέω) gladness (εὐφροσύνη). For through you we have been loosed from bonds (δεσμά) of death. Come here to us, O divine and life-bearing (ζωηφόρος) treasure (κειμήλιον). Come to us longing (ποθέω), you who accomplished (ἐκπεραίνω) our longing (πόθος). But the multitude (πληθύς) of saints standing around in the body drew back the other way (ἀνθέλκω) with words not weaker, saying: Stay (μένω) with us, our consolation, the only comfort on earth of ours. Do not leave (ἐάω) us orphans (ὀρφανοί), O Mother, running danger ahead for your compassionate (συμπαθής) Son. May we have you as respite (ἀνάπαυλα) of labours and unfolding/relief (ἀνάπτυξις) of sweats (ἱδρῶτες). To you, both wishing to stay, the ability is present, and eager to depart (ἀπαίρω), nothing [is] a hindrance (ἐμπόδιον). If you depart, the tent (σκηνή) of God, may we also depart with [you], having been called (χρηματίζω) your people (λαός) because of your Son. You alone left (καταλείπω) to us on earth [as] consolation (παρηγορία) we possess. With you living to live together (συζάω), and dying to die together (συνθνῄσκω), [is] blessed. But why do we say dying? For to you both life and death [are] — and better (κρείττων) life, and surpassing (ὑπεραίρω) this life by incomparable comparisons; but to us how [is] life (βίος) unlivable (ἀβίωτος), not having you as companion (συνόμιλος)?
pass_b_english: Then, yes then, Adam and Eve, the forebears of our race, cried aloud with rejoicing lips: 'Blessed daughter, you have undone for us the penalties of our transgression. You inherited from us a body subject to corruption, and you bore in your womb a garment of incorruption for us. You took your being from our loins, and you gave us well-being in return. You put an end to the pangs; you tore apart the swaddling bands of death; you restored us to our ancient dwelling. We shut paradise; you threw open the entrance to the tree of life. Through us sorrows came out of good things; through you better things have come back to us out of sorrows. And how will you taste death, you who are spotless? For you death will become a bridge to life, a ladder to heaven, a ferry to immortality. Truly you are blessed, all-blessed one. For who, unless it be the Word, has offered himself to undergo the very thing he was supposed to be doing?' And the whole choir of the saints applauded: 'You have fulfilled our prophecies. You have brought us the joy we waited for. For through you we have been loosed from the bonds of death. Come to us, O divine and life-bearing treasure. Come to us who long for you, you who brought our longing to fulfilment.' But the crowd of saints still in the body, standing around her, pulled her back with words no less strong: 'Stay with us,' they said, 'you who are our consolation, our only comfort on earth. Do not leave us orphans (John 14:18), O Mother, as we face dangers for your compassionate Son. Let us have you as rest from our labours and relief from our sweat. If you wish to stay, you have the power; if you are eager to depart, nothing stands in your way. If you depart, tabernacle of God, may we too depart with you, we who have been called your people because of your Son. You alone are the consolation we have, left to us on earth. To live with you while you live, and to die with you as you die, is a blessed thing. But why do we say "as you die"? For you, death too is life, and a better life, one that surpasses this life beyond all comparison. But for us, how life is no life at all, if we do not have you with us!'

choices.note: John 14:18 ('I will not leave you orphans') is a clear allusion.
Possible echoes left uncited as uncertain: the ladder to heaven (Genesis 28:12), 'stay with us' (Luke 24:29), the shut paradise (Genesis 3:23–24).
Doubtful sense: 'For who, unless it be the Word, has offered himself to undergo the very thing he was supposed to be doing?' (τίς ...
προσενήνεκται τοῦτο πάσχων, ὃ πράττειν ὑπείληπται) is obscure; it seems to say that, like the Word, she undergoes the death she undoes.
προσενήνεκται is taken as middle ('offered himself'), as the facing Latin does ('ad hoc tolerandum se obtulerit, quod patrasse censitus sit').
The English keeps the riddle rather than resolving it.
'For you, death too is life, and a better life' renders 'σοὶ μὲν γὰρ ἡ ζωὴ καὶ ὁ θάνατος, καὶ ζωὴ κρείττων', taking death as subject and life as predicate;
Germ. reads ζωῆς for ζωὴ before κρείττων.
ἀνάπτυξις ('unfolding') is rendered 'relief'; a possible reading ἀνάψυξις ('refreshment') would give the same sense.
'As we face dangers for your compassionate Son' renders προκινδυνεύοντας, literally 'running risks in front, on behalf of'.

'You put an end to the pangs' (τὰς ὠδῖνας ἔλυσας) leaves the pangs unspecified as the Greek does (facing Latin 'dolores solvisti'); it may echo Acts 2:24 ('having loosed the pangs of death'), left uncited as uncertain.
The facing Latin also takes 'death is life, and a better life' this way ('tibi namque mors vita est, imo vita praestantior').
